This is from Google AI:
\ProjectDeepHeading{9}{Point-wise Transformers}
    
    Point-wise Transformers (often referred to as \textbf{Point Transformers}) are neural network architectures that adapt the standard Transformer self-attention mechanism to process 3D point cloud data.
    
    \ProjectDeepHeading{10}{Key Concepts}
        \begin{itemize}
            \item \textbf{Permutation Invariance:} Unlike sequences in NLP, 3D point clouds are unordered sets. Point-wise Transformers are designed to be invariant to the order of points, ensuring the output is the same regardless of how the points are indexed.
            \item \textbf{Vector Self-Attention:} Instead of the standard scalar dot-product attention used in language models, many Point Transformers use vector self-attention. This allows the model to modulate each feature channel individually, which is more effective for capturing the high-dimensional geometric features of 3D data.
            \item \textbf{Local Neighborhood Processing:} Because global self-attention on large point clouds is computationally expensive (quadratic complexity), these models often perform attention within local neighborhoods defined by k-nearest neighbors (k-NN).
        \end{itemize}
    
    \ProjectDeepHeading{10}{Typical Architecture Blocks}
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item \textbf{Point Transformer Block:} The core unit that performs self-attention between points to learn local and global features.
            \item \textbf{Transition Down Block:} Reduces the number of points (downsampling) while increasing feature dimensions, similar to pooling in CNNs.
            \item \textbf{Transition Up Block:} Restores the point density for tasks requiring per-point predictions, such as semantic segmentation.
            \item \textbf{Relative Position Encoding:} Uses the 3D coordinates ($x, y, z$) of points to encode spatial relationships, often by passing the relative offsets between points through a small MLP.
        \end{enumerate}
    
    \ProjectDeepHeading{10}{Primary Applications}
        \begin{itemize}
            \item \textbf{3D Object Classification:} Identifying what an object is from a raw point cloud.
            \item \textbf{Semantic Segmentation:} Labeling every individual point in a 3D scene (e.g., distinguishing a "chair" point from a "floor" point).
            \item \textbf{Part Segmentation:} Breaking down an object into its constituent parts (e.g., the legs, seat, and back of a chair).
            \item \textbf{Point Cloud Registration:} Aligning two different 3D scans of the same object or environment.
        \end{itemize}
    
    \ProjectDeepHeading{10}{Related Terms}
        \begin{itemize}
            \item \textbf{Position-Wise Feed-Forward Network:} In standard Transformer models (like GPT), this refers to the sub-layer that processes each token independently after the attention step.
            \item \textbf{Fast Point Transformer (FPT):} An optimized version that uses techniques like sparse voxelization to speed up processing for large-scale 3D scenes.
        \end{itemize}

\ProjectDeepHeading{5}{Uncertainty}

% Source: nd_datascience_learning_project/machine_learning/model/architecture/neural_network/kind/deep_learning/kind/transformer/kind/uncertainty/uncertainty.tex

\ProjectDeepHeading{8}{Introduction}
        
        Transformer-based models have been used for time-series forecasting because self-attention can model temporal dependencies over sequences. In deterministic forecasting, the model usually predicts only one future value for each output time step. However, in uncertainty-aware forecasting, the model predicts a probability distribution over future values.
        
        The model described here is a Gaussian Transformer for uncertainty-aware time-series forecasting. For each output time step and each output feature, it predicts two Gaussian parameters: the mean and the log-variance.
        
        The general forecasting problem is
        
        \[
            f_{\ensuremath{\theta}}:
            \mathbb{R}^{T_{\mathrm{in}} \times F_{\mathrm{in}}}
            \rightarrow
            \mathbb{R}^{T_{\mathrm{out}} \times 2F_{\mathrm{out}}},
        \]
        
        where \(T_{\mathrm{in}}\) is the input horizon, \(T_{\mathrm{out}}\) is the output horizon, \(F_{\mathrm{in}}\) is the number of input features, and \(F_{\mathrm{out}}\) is the number of output features.
        
        The factor \(2F_{\mathrm{out}}\) appears because the model predicts two values for each output feature:
        
        \[
            \ensuremath{\mu}
            \quad
            \text{and}
            \quad
            \log \ensuremath{\sigma}^2.
        \]
        
        This formulation is related to probabilistic Transformer-based forecasting. For example, \cite{jawed-2022-gqformer-a-multi-quantile-generative-transformer-for-time-series-forecasting} proposed GQFormer, a Transformer-based probabilistic forecasting model that represents uncertainty through multiple forecast quantiles instead of producing only point predictions. In contrast, the present model represents uncertainty through a Gaussian predictive distribution.
    
    
    \ProjectDeepHeading{8}{Input and Target Time-Series Windows}
        
        Let the original time series be
        
        \[
            S
            =
            \left[
                s_1,
                s_2,
                \ldots,
            s_N
            \right],
        \]
        
        where
        
        \[
            s_i
            \in
            \mathbb{R}^{F}.
        \]
        
        For each window index \(k\), the input window is
        
        \[
            X^{(k)}
            =
            \left[
                x_k,
                x_{k+1},
                \ldots,
            x_{k+T_{\mathrm{in}}-1}
            \right],
        \]
        
        where
        
        \[
            x_t
            \in
            \mathbb{R}^{F_{\mathrm{in}}}.
        \]
        
        The corresponding target window is
        
        \[
            Y^{(k)}
            =
            \left[
                y_{k+T_{\mathrm{in}}},
            y_{k+T_{\mathrm{in}}+1},
                \ldots,
            y_{k+T_{\mathrm{in}}+T_{\mathrm{out}}-1}
            \right],
        \]
        
        where
        
        \[
            y_t
            \in
            \mathbb{R}^{F_{\mathrm{out}}}.
        \]
        
        For a batch of input windows, the input tensor has the shape
        
        \[
            X
            \in
            \mathbb{R}^{B \times T_{\mathrm{in}} \times F_{\mathrm{in}}},
        \]
        
        where \(B\) is the batch size.
        
        The target tensor has the shape
        
        \[
            Y
            \in
            \mathbb{R}^{B \times T_{\mathrm{out}} \times F_{\mathrm{out}}}.
        \]
    
    
    \ProjectDeepHeading{8}{Input Projection and Positional Embedding}
        
        The input sequence is first projected into the Transformer model dimension. Let \(d_{\mathrm{model}}\) denote the latent model dimension. The input projection is
        
        \[
            H_0
            =
            XW_{\mathrm{in}}
            +
            b_{\mathrm{in}},
        \]
        
        where
        
        \[
            H_0
            \in
            \mathbb{R}^{B \times T_{\mathrm{in}} \times d_{\mathrm{model}}}.
        \]
        
        Since the Transformer has no recurrent structure, positional information is added to the projected sequence. A learnable positional embedding \(P\) is added as
        
        \[
            H
            =
            H_0
            +
            P.
        \]
        
        Here,
        
        \[
            P
            \in
            \mathbb{R}^{T_{\mathrm{in}} \times d_{\mathrm{model}}}.
        \]
        
        This allows the model to distinguish between different temporal positions in the input window.
    
    
    \ProjectDeepHeading{8}{Self-Attention Layer}
        
        The Transformer uses self-attention to model temporal dependencies between different time steps. From the hidden representation \(H\), the query, key, and value matrices are computed as
        
        \[
            Q
            =
            HW_Q,
        \]
        
        \[
            K
            =
            HW_K,
        \]
        
        \[
            V
            =
            HW_V.
        \]
        
        For one attention head, the scaled dot-product attention is
        
        \[
            \mathrm{Attention}
            \left(
                Q,
                K,
                V
            \right)
            =
            \mathrm{softmax}
            \left(
                \frac{
                    QK^{\top}
                }{
                    \sqrt{d_k}
                }
            \right)
            V,
        \]
        
        where \(d_k\) is the key dimension. If \(h\) is the number of attention heads, then
        
        \[
            d_k
            =
            \frac{
                d_{\mathrm{model}}
            }{
                h
            }.
        \]
        
        Multi-head attention applies this operation over several heads:
        
        \[
            \mathrm{MHA}(H)
            =
            \mathrm{Concat}
            \left(
                \mathrm{head}_1,
                \mathrm{head}_2,
                \ldots,
                \mathrm{head}_h
            \right)
            W_O.
        \]
        
        The output of the attention layer is added to the input representation through a residual connection and then normalized:
        
        \[
            H_{\mathrm{attn}}
            =
            \mathrm{LayerNorm}
            \left(
                H
                +
                \mathrm{Dropout}
                \left(
                    \mathrm{MHA}(H)
                \right)
            \right).
        \]
    
    
    \ProjectDeepHeading{8}{Feed-Forward Layer}
        
        After self-attention, the model applies a position-wise feed-forward network. This network is applied independently to each time step:
        
        \[
            \mathrm{FFN}
            \left(
                H_{\mathrm{attn}}
            \right)
            =
            \ensuremath{\phi}
            \left(
                H_{\mathrm{attn}}W_1
            +
            b_1
            \right)
            W_2
            +
            b_2,
        \]
        
        where \(\ensuremath{\phi}\) is the ReLU activation function.
        
        The feed-forward output is again added through a residual connection and normalized:
        
        \[
            H_{\mathrm{enc}}
            =
            \mathrm{LayerNorm}
            \left(
                H_{\mathrm{attn}}
                +
                \mathrm{Dropout}
                \left(
                    \mathrm{FFN}
                    \left(
                        H_{\mathrm{attn}}
                    \right)
                \right)
            \right).
        \]
        
        The tensor \(H_{\mathrm{enc}}\) is the encoded representation of the input time-series window.
    
    
    \ProjectDeepHeading{8}{Mapping from Input Horizon to Output Horizon}
        
        In a general time-series forecasting formulation, the input horizon and the output horizon do not need to be equal. Therefore, after encoding the input sequence, the model should produce an output sequence of length \(T_{\mathrm{out}}\).
        
        Conceptually, this can be written as
        
        \[
            Z
            =
            g_{\ensuremath{\theta}}
            \left(
                H_{\mathrm{enc}}
            \right),
        \]
        
        where
        
        \[
            Z
            \in
            \mathbb{R}^{B \times T_{\mathrm{out}} \times d_{\mathrm{model}}}.
        \]
        
        The function \(g_{\ensuremath{\theta}}\) represents the part of the model that maps the encoded input horizon to the prediction horizon. This mapping can be implemented in different ways, for example by using a decoder, learned output queries, temporal pooling followed by projection, or another sequence-mapping layer.
        
        The important point is that the general forecasting model should learn the mapping
        
        \[
            \mathbb{R}^{B \times T_{\mathrm{in}} \times F_{\mathrm{in}}}
            \rightarrow
            \mathbb{R}^{B \times T_{\mathrm{out}} \times 2F_{\mathrm{out}}},
        \]
        
        not necessarily
        
        \[
            \mathbb{R}^{B \times T_{\mathrm{out}} \times F_{\mathrm{in}}}
            \rightarrow
            \mathbb{R}^{B \times T_{\mathrm{out}} \times 2F_{\mathrm{out}}}.
        \]
    
    
    \ProjectDeepHeading{8}{Gaussian Output Layer}
        
        The probabilistic output layer predicts two tensors. The first tensor is the mean:
        
        \[
            \ensuremath{\mu}
            =
            f_{\ensuremath{\mu}}
            \left(
                Z
            \right),
        \]
        
        and the second tensor is the log-variance:
        
        \[
            \log \ensuremath{\sigma}^2
            =
            f_{\log \ensuremath{\sigma}^2}
            \left(
                Z
            \right).
        \]
        
        Both tensors have the shape
        
        \[
            \ensuremath{\mu},
            \log \ensuremath{\sigma}^2
            \in
            \mathbb{R}^{B \times T_{\mathrm{out}} \times F_{\mathrm{out}}}.
        \]
        
        The final output of the model is the concatenation of these two tensors:
        
        \[
            \hat{Y}_{\mathrm{params}}
            =
            \left[
                \ensuremath{\mu},
                \log \ensuremath{\sigma}^2
            \right].
        \]
        
        Therefore,
        
        \[
            \hat{Y}_{\mathrm{params}}
            \in
            \mathbb{R}^{B \times T_{\mathrm{out}} \times 2F_{\mathrm{out}}}.
        \]
        
        The predicted variance is recovered from the predicted log-variance as
        
        \[
            \ensuremath{\sigma}^2
            =
            \exp
            \left(
                \log \ensuremath{\sigma}^2
            \right).
        \]
        
        This transformation guarantees that the variance remains positive.
    
    
    \ProjectDeepHeading{8}{Probabilistic Interpretation}
        
        For each batch item \(b\), output time step \(t\), and output feature \(j\), the model assumes that the target value follows a Gaussian distribution:
        
        \[
            y_{b,t,j}
            \sim
            \mathcal{N}
            \left(
                \ensuremath{\mu}_{b,t,j},
                \ensuremath{\sigma}^2_{b,t,j}
            \right).
        \]
        
        Equivalently, the conditional predictive distribution is
        
        \[
            p
            \left(
                y_{b,t,j}
                \mid
                X_b
            \right)
            =
            \mathcal{N}
            \left(
                y_{b,t,j};
                \ensuremath{\mu}_{b,t,j},
                \ensuremath{\sigma}^2_{b,t,j}
            \right).
        \]
        
        The mean \(\ensuremath{\mu}_{b,t,j}\) represents the expected future value:
        
        \[
            \ensuremath{\mu}_{b,t,j}
            \approx
            \mathbb{E}
            \left[
                y_{b,t,j}
                \mid
                X_b
            \right],
        \]
        
        while the variance \(\ensuremath{\sigma}^2_{b,t,j}\) represents predictive uncertainty:
        
        \[
            \ensuremath{\sigma}^2_{b,t,j}
            \approx
            \mathrm{Var}
            \left(
                y_{b,t,j}
                \mid
                X_b
            \right).
        \]
        
        A small variance indicates that the model is relatively confident about its prediction. A large variance indicates higher predictive uncertainty.
    
    
    \ProjectDeepHeading{8}{Gaussian Negative Log-Likelihood Loss}
        
        The model is trained using the Gaussian negative log-likelihood. For a scalar target value \(y\), the Gaussian likelihood is
        
        \[
            p
            \left(
                y
                \mid
                \ensuremath{\mu},
                \ensuremath{\sigma}^2
            \right)
            =
            \frac{
                1
            }{
                \sqrt{
                    2\ensuremath{\pi}\ensuremath{\sigma}^2
                }
            }
            \exp
            \left(
                -
                \frac{
                    \left(
                        y
                        -
                        \ensuremath{\mu}
                    \right)^2
                }{
                    2\ensuremath{\sigma}^2
                }
            \right).
        \]
        
        The negative log-likelihood is
        
        \[
            -
            \log
            p
            \left(
                y
                \mid
                \ensuremath{\mu},
                \ensuremath{\sigma}^2
            \right)
            =
            \frac{1}{2}
            \log
            \left(
                2\ensuremath{\pi}\ensuremath{\sigma}^2
            \right)
            +
            \frac{
                \left(
                    y
                    -
                    \ensuremath{\mu}
                \right)^2
            }{
                2\ensuremath{\sigma}^2
            }.
        \]
        
        The constant term \(\frac{1}{2}\log(2\ensuremath{\pi})\) does not affect optimization. Therefore, the implemented loss uses the simplified form
        
        \[
            \mathcal{L}_{b,t,j}
            =
            \frac{1}{2}
            \left[
                \log \ensuremath{\sigma}^2_{b,t,j}
                +
                \frac{
                    \left(
                        y_{b,t,j}
                        -
                        \ensuremath{\mu}_{b,t,j}
                    \right)^2
                }{
                    \ensuremath{\sigma}^2_{b,t,j}
                }
            \right].
        \]
        
        Since the model predicts \(\log \ensuremath{\sigma}^2\), the inverse variance can be written as
        
        \[
            \frac{1}{\ensuremath{\sigma}^2_{b,t,j}}
            =
            \exp
            \left(
                -
                \log \ensuremath{\sigma}^2_{b,t,j}
            \right).
        \]
        
        Therefore, the implemented loss is
        
        \[
            \mathcal{L}_{b,t,j}
            =
            \frac{1}{2}
            \left[
                \log \ensuremath{\sigma}^2_{b,t,j}
                +
                \left(
                    y_{b,t,j}
                    -
                    \ensuremath{\mu}_{b,t,j}
                \right)^2
                \exp
                \left(
                    -
                    \log \ensuremath{\sigma}^2_{b,t,j}
                \right)
            \right].
        \]
        
        For one output time step, the loss is summed over all output features:
        
        \[
            \mathcal{L}_{b,t}
            =
            \sum_{j=1}^{F_{\mathrm{out}}}
            \mathcal{L}_{b,t,j}.
        \]
        
        The final loss is the mean over all batch items and output time steps:
        
        \[
            \mathcal{L}
            =
            \frac{1}{BT_{\mathrm{out}}}
            \sum_{b=1}^{B}
            \sum_{t=1}^{T_{\mathrm{out}}}
            \sum_{j=1}^{F_{\mathrm{out}}}
            \frac{1}{2}
            \left[
                \log \ensuremath{\sigma}^2_{b,t,j}
                +
                \left(
                    y_{b,t,j}
                    -
                    \ensuremath{\mu}_{b,t,j}
                \right)^2
                \exp
                \left(
                    -
                    \log \ensuremath{\sigma}^2_{b,t,j}
                \right)
            \right].
        \]
    
    
    \ProjectDeepHeading{8}{Sliding Window Training Pairs}
        
        The training data are generated from the original time series using a sliding window. For each window index \(k\), the input sequence is
        
        \[
            X^{(k)}
            =
            \left[
                s_k,
                s_{k+1},
                \ldots,
            s_{k+T_{\mathrm{in}}-1}
            \right].
        \]
        
        The corresponding target sequence is
        
        \[
            Y^{(k)}
            =
            \left[
                s_{k+T_{\mathrm{in}}},
            s_{k+T_{\mathrm{in}}+1},
                \ldots,
            s_{k+T_{\mathrm{in}}+T_{\mathrm{out}}-1}
            \right].
        \]
        
        If an overlap value \(O\) is used between consecutive input-target pairs, the next window starts before the previous window has fully moved away. This increases the number of training examples and allows neighboring temporal patterns to be represented in the training set.
        
        The training dataset can be written as
        
        \[
            \mathcal{D}
            =
            \left\{
                \left(
                    X^{(k)},
                Y^{(k)}
                \right)
            \right\}_{k=1}^{M}.
        \]
    
    
    \ProjectDeepHeading{8}{Meaning of Uncertainty}
        
        The predicted mean gives the expected future value:
        
        \[
            \ensuremath{\mu}_{b,t,j}
            \approx
            \mathbb{E}
            \left[
                y_{b,t,j}
                \mid
                X_b
            \right].
        \]
        
        The predicted variance gives the predictive uncertainty:
        
        \[
            \ensuremath{\sigma}^2_{b,t,j}
            \approx
            \mathrm{Var}
            \left(
                y_{b,t,j}
                \mid
                X_b
            \right).
        \]
        
        The standard deviation is
        
        \[
            \ensuremath{\sigma}_{b,t,j}
            =
            \sqrt{
                \ensuremath{\sigma}^2_{b,t,j}
            }.
        \]
        
        Assuming a Gaussian predictive distribution, an approximate 95 percent prediction interval is
        
        \[
            y_{b,t,j}
            \in
            \left[
                \ensuremath{\mu}_{b,t,j}
                -
                1.96\ensuremath{\sigma}_{b,t,j},
                \ensuremath{\mu}_{b,t,j}
                +
                1.96\ensuremath{\sigma}_{b,t,j}
            \right].
        \]
        
        This interval gives an interpretable range around the predicted mean. Wider intervals indicate larger predictive uncertainty.
    
    
    \ProjectDeepHeading{8}{Simplification in the Current Implementation}
        
        The general formulation distinguishes between the input horizon \(T_{\mathrm{in}}\) and the output horizon \(T_{\mathrm{out}}\). However, the current implementation uses the output sequence size as the input sequence length in the TensorFlow input layer.
        
        Therefore, the current implementation implicitly uses
        
        \[
            X
            \in
            \mathbb{R}^{B \times T_{\mathrm{out}} \times F_{\mathrm{in}}},
        \]
        
        and assumes
        
        \[
            T_{\mathrm{in}}
            =
            T_{\mathrm{out}}.
        \]
        
        This equality is not a theoretical requirement of the Gaussian Transformer. It is only a simplifying assumption in the current implementation.
        
        A more general implementation should define the input tensor as
        
        \[
            X
            \in
            \mathbb{R}^{B \times T_{\mathrm{in}} \times F_{\mathrm{in}}},
        \]
        
        and the output tensor as
        
        \[
            \hat{Y}_{\mathrm{params}}
            \in
            \mathbb{R}^{B \times T_{\mathrm{out}} \times 2F_{\mathrm{out}}}.
        \]
    
    
    \ProjectDeepHeading{8}{Summary}
        
        The model is an uncertainty-aware Transformer for time-series forecasting. It receives an input time-series window and predicts a future output window. For each future time step and each output feature, it predicts a Gaussian mean and a Gaussian variance.
        
        The predicted mean represents the expected future value, while the predicted variance represents predictive uncertainty. The model is trained using the Gaussian negative log-likelihood, which encourages the model to predict accurate means and meaningful uncertainty estimates.
        
        The current implementation simplifies the general formulation by assuming equal input and output horizons. However, the general mathematical formulation should keep \(T_{\mathrm{in}}\) and \(T_{\mathrm{out}}\) separate.

\subsubsection{Discrepancy detection}

% Source: nd_datascience_learning_project/machine_learning/model/discrepancy_detection/discrepancy_detection.tex

% ND_MIND_MIRROR_CONTENT

% Source: nd_datascience_learning_project/machine_learning/model/discrepancy_detection/anomaly_vs_outlier_vs_novelty_noise.tex

\begin{itemize}

        \item \textbf{Outlier:}

        An outlier is an observation that deviates markedly from other members
        of the sample or appears inconsistent with the remainder of the data
        \cite{hodge-austin-2004-a-survey-of-outlier-detection-methodologies}.

        Outlierness is primarily characterized through statistical properties
        such as distance, density, probability, or deviation from the dominant
        structure of the data.

        An outlier does not necessarily represent an error or an invalid
        observation; it may result from measurement error, system faults, noise,
        or simply a rare but valid natural variation
        \cite{hodge-austin-2004-a-survey-of-outlier-detection-methodologies}.

        \item \textbf{Anomaly:}

        An anomaly is an observation, behavior, or pattern that does not conform
        to a well-defined notion of expected or normal behavior
        \cite{chandola-banerjee-kumar-2009-anomaly-detection-a-survey}.

        Depending on the application, an anomaly may correspond to a fault,
        intrusion, fraud, malfunction, or another event that is relevant to the
        system or analyst.

        Anomalies are not restricted to isolated extreme points; they may be
        point anomalies, contextual anomalies, or collective patterns whose
        abnormality emerges from their context or their relationships with other
        observations
        \cite{chandola-banerjee-kumar-2009-anomaly-detection-a-survey}.

        \item \textbf{Novelty:}

        Novelty detection is the task of identifying test observations that
        differ from the data available during training
        \cite{pimentel-clifton-clifton-tarassenko-2014-a-review-of-novelty-detection}.

        It is commonly formulated as a one-class classification problem in which a model of normality is constructed from training data that predominantly, or ideally exclusively, represent normal behavior.

        A novel observation therefore represents a previously unseen pattern relative to the learned model of normality. Unlike an anomaly, a detected
        novelty may subsequently be incorporated into the model of normal behavior if it is determined to represent a valid new regime \cite{pimentel-clifton-clifton-tarassenko-2014-a-review-of-novelty-detection,chandola-banerjee-kumar-2009-anomaly-detection-a-survey}.

    \end{itemize}

\paragraph{Anomaly}

% Source: nd_datascience_learning_project/machine_learning/model/discrepancy_detection/anomaly/anomaly.tex

anomaly detection is generally understood to be the identification of rare items, events or observations which deviate significantly from the majority of the data and do not conform to a well defined notion of normal behavior \seeherefooter{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anomaly_detection}.

\paragraph{Novelty}

% Source: nd_datascience_learning_project/machine_learning/model/discrepancy_detection/novelty/novelty.tex

Novelty detection is described as a neural function that determines whether an incoming stimulus is familiar or novel.
   The paper argues that such mechanisms are widespread in the central nervous system and participate in several cognitive functions. It proposes and simulates several neural novelty-detector models. A bi-compartmental model reproduces neural novelty-detection behavior particularly well and resembles cortical architecture, especially area 17. The model assumes that novelty detection begins with retrieving stored information and comparing it with incoming input \cite{salu-1988-models-of-neural-novelty-detectors-with-similarities-to-cerebral-cortex}

   Novelty detection is the mechanism by which an intelligent organism is able to identify an incoming sensory pattern as being so far unknown. If the pattern is sufficiently salient or associated with a high positive or strong negative utility, it will be given computational resources for effective future processing \seeherefooter{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novelty_detection}.

\paragraph{Outlier}

% Source: nd_datascience_learning_project/machine_learning/model/discrepancy_detection/outlier/outlier.tex

In statistics, an outlier is a data point that differs significantly from other observations \seeherefooter{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outlier}

\paragraph{Regression}

\subparagraph{Root mean squared error}

% Source: nd_datascience_learning_project/machine_learning/model/evaluation/regression/root_mean_squared_error/root_mean_squared_error.tex

Root Mean Squared Error, abbreviated as RMSE, is a measure of the average magnitude of prediction error. It is commonly used to evaluate how far predicted values are from true values.
    
    Assume that the true values are
    
    \[
        y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n
    \]
    
    and the fitted or predicted values are
    
    \[
        \hat{y}_1, \hat{y}_2, \ldots, \hat{y}_n
    \]
    
    The error at each point is
    
    \[
        e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i
    \]
    
    The RMSE is defined as
    
    \[
        \mathrm{RMSE}
        =
        \sqrt{
            \frac{1}{n}
            \sum_{i=1}^{n}
            (
            y_i - \hat{y}_i
            )^2
        }
    \]
    
    RMSE first squares each error, then computes the mean of the squared errors, and finally takes the square root. Because the errors are squared, RMSE gives more weight to large errors than Mean Absolute Error.
    
    For example, suppose the true values are
    
    \[
        y = [10, 12, 15]
    \]
    
    and the predicted values are
    
    \[
        \hat{y} = [9, 14, 14]
    \]
    
    The errors are
    
    \[
        e = y - \hat{y} = [1, -2, 1]
    \]
    
    Therefore,
    
    \[
        \mathrm{RMSE}
        =
        \sqrt{
            \frac{
                1^2 + (-2)^2 + 1^2
            }{3}
        }
    \]
    
    \[
        \mathrm{RMSE}
        =
        \sqrt{
            \frac{6}{3}
        }
        =
        \sqrt{2}
        \approx 1.414
    \]
    
    In this example, the RMSE is approximately \(1.414\). This means that the predicted values differ from the true values by about \(1.414\) units on average, with larger errors having stronger influence on the final value.

Because it describes a full data-generating process, a generative model can be used to draw new samples that resemble the observed data, a process often referred to as synthetic data generation.

\subsection{Auto correlation}

% Source: nd_datascience_learning_project/signal_processing/auto_correlation/auto_correlation.tex

Autocorrelation, sometimes known as serial correlation in the discrete time case, measures the correlation of a signal with a delayed copy of itself. \url{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autocorrelation}

% Source: nd_datascience_learning_project/signal_processing/auto_correlation/fast_fourier_transform.tex

\subparagraph{Definition}
   Berberidis et al. propose a method for detecting weak periodicities in large time-series data when the period is not    known in advance \cite{berberidis-2002-on-the-discovery-of-weak-periodicities-in-large-time-series}. The method combines the autocorrelation function with the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) to identify approximate periodic behavior. FFT provides an efficient frequency-domain representation that helps identify candidate periodic components. Autocorrelation is then used to characterize repeating patterns in the time series. The approach enables period discovery without requiring the period length to be specified beforehand.
   
   A fast Fourier transform (FFT) is an algorithm that computes the discrete Fourier transform (DFT), or its inverse (IDFT), of a sequence. A Fourier transform converts a signal from its original domain (often time or space) to a representation in the frequency domain and vice versa \seeherefooter{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast_Fourier_transform}.

\section{Geometry}

\subsection{Polygon}

\subsubsection{Centroid}

% Source: nd_math_learning_project/geometry/polygon/centroid/centroid.tex

\ProjectDeepHeading{1}{Centroid of a Polygon}
        
        For a polygon with \(q\) vertices
        \(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \dots, \mathbf{v}_q \in \mathbb{R}^{n}\),
        the simplest centroid is computed as the arithmetic mean of its vertices.
        This centroid represents the average position of all polygon vertices in the
        \(n\)-dimensional space.
        
        \[
            \mathbf{c}
            =
            \frac{1}{q}
            \sum_{i=1}^{q}
            \mathbf{v}_i,
            \qquad
            \mathbf{v}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{n}
        \]
        
        If the polygon is considered as a filled planar shape, the geometric centroid
        can be computed by decomposing the polygon into \(q-2\) triangles. In this case,
        the centroid is the area-weighted average of the centroids of those triangles.
        
        \[
            \mathbf{c}
            =
            \frac{
                \sum_{i=1}^{q-2}
                A_i
                \bigg(
                \frac{
                    \mathbf{v}_1
                    +
                    \mathbf{v}_{i+1}
                    +
                    \mathbf{v}_{i+2}
                }{3}
                \bigg)
            }{
                \sum_{i=1}^{q-2}
                A_i
            }
        \]
        
        Here, \(A_i\) is the area of the triangle formed by
        \(\mathbf{v}_1\), \(\mathbf{v}_{i+1}\), and \(\mathbf{v}_{i+2}\).
        
        \[
            A_i
            =
            \frac{1}{2}
            \sqrt{
                \lVert \mathbf{v}_{i+1} - \mathbf{v}_1 \rVert^2
                \lVert \mathbf{v}_{i+2} - \mathbf{v}_1 \rVert^2
                -
                \bigg(
                \big(
                \mathbf{v}_{i+1} - \mathbf{v}_1
                \big)^{\top}
                \big(
                \mathbf{v}_{i+2} - \mathbf{v}_1
                \big)
                \bigg)^2
            }
        \]
        
        For two-dimensional polygons, the same geometric centroid can also be written
        directly using the signed area of the polygon.
        
        \[
            A
            =
            \frac{1}{2}
            \sum_{i=1}^{q}
            \big(
            x_i y_{i+1}
            -
            x_{i+1} y_i
            \big)
        \]
        
        \[
            C_x
            =
            \frac{1}{6A}
            \sum_{i=1}^{q}
            \big(
            x_i + x_{i+1}
            \big)
            \big(
            x_i y_{i+1}
            -
            x_{i+1} y_i
            \big)
        \]
        
        \[
            C_y
            =
            \frac{1}{6A}
            \sum_{i=1}^{q}
            \big(
            y_i + y_{i+1}
            \big)
            \big(
            x_i y_{i+1}
            -
            x_{i+1} y_i
            \big)
        \]
        
        Here,
        
        \[
            x_{q+1} = x_1,
            \qquad
            y_{q+1} = y_1.
        \]
        
        Therefore, the two-dimensional geometric centroid is
        
        \[
            \mathbf{c}
            =
            \begin{bmatrix}
                C_x \\
                C_y
            \end{bmatrix}.
        \]

\section{Probability}

\subsection{Bayesian}

% Source: nd_math_learning_project/probability/bayesian/bayesian.tex

{\Large\bfseries Bayesian Inference}\par
\medskip
Bayesian inference is the process of updating beliefs about a hypothesis when new data is observed.
    
    \bigskip
    {\bfseries Bayes' Theorem}\par
    \begin{equation*}
        P(H \mid D)
        =
        \frac{P(D \mid H)\,P(H)}{P(D)}
    \end{equation*}
    
    \bigskip
    {\bfseries Proportional Form}\par
    \begin{equation*}
        P(H \mid D) \propto P(D \mid H)\,P(H)
    \end{equation*}

% Source: nd_math_learning_project/probability/bayesian/evidence.tex

\bigskip
    {\bfseries Evidence (Normalization)}\par
    The total probability of observing the data.\par
    \begin{equation*}
        \textbf{Evidence:}\quad
        P(D) = \sum_{h} P(D \mid h)\,P(h)
    \end{equation*}
    (For continuous hypotheses, replace the sum by an integral.)\par

% Source: nd_math_learning_project/probability/bayesian/likelihood.tex

\bigskip
    {\bfseries Likelihood}\par
    The probability of observing the data assuming the hypothesis is true.\par
    \begin{equation*}
        \textbf{Likelihood:}\quad P(D \mid H)
    \end{equation*}
    Likelihood is not the probability of the hypothesis.\par

\subsubsection{Belief}

% Source: nd_math_learning_project/probability/bayesian/belief/belief.tex

{\bfseries Belief}\par
        Belief is the current probability distribution over hypotheses.\\
        for example: hypothesis: \quote{It rains now} the belife is is a
        \begin{equation*}
            \mathrm{Belief}(H) =
            \begin{cases}
                P(H) & \text{(prior belief)} \\
                P(H \mid D) & \text{(posterior belief)}
            \end{cases}
        \end{equation*}

% Source: nd_math_learning_project/probability/bayesian/belief/posterior.tex

\bigskip
    {\bfseries Posterior or posterior belief}\par
    The updated belief about the hypothesis after observing data.\par
    \begin{equation*}
        \textbf{Posterior:}\quad P(H \mid D)
    \end{equation*}

% Source: nd_math_learning_project/probability/bayesian/belief/prior.tex

{\bfseries Prior or perior belief}\par
    The belief about a hypothesis before observing data.\par
    \begin{equation*}
        \textbf{Prior:}\quad P(H)
    \end{equation*}

\subsection{Distribution}

% Source: nd_math_learning_project/probability/distribution/distribution.tex

A probability distribution is:
A mathematical object that assigns probabilities to events.
Formally:
\begin{itemize}
    \item Discrete case: assigns probabilities to points
    \item Continuous case: assigns probabilities to sets (intervals)
\end{itemize}
It is not necessarily a function you can write as a formula.
Examples:
\begin{itemize}
    \item “A fair die”
    \item “A Gaussian with mean 0 and variance 1”
    \item “The posterior over hypotheses”
\end{itemize}

All of these are distributions, even before you choose a formula.

\paragraph{Kind}

\subparagraph{Distance}

\ProjectDeepHeading{1}{Kind}

\ProjectDeepHeading{2}{Mahalanobis}

% Source: nd_math_learning_project/probability/distribution/discrepency/kind/distance/kind/mahalanobis/mahalanobis.tex

The Mahalanobis distance measures the distance of a point from a distribution by
    taking the covariance structure of the data into account \citep{mahalanobis-1936-on-the-generalised-distance-in-statistics}.
    It can be interpreted as a covariance-normalized generalization of the Euclidean
    distance \citep{de-maesschalck-2000-the-mahalanobis-distance}.

\ProjectDeepHeading{2}{Wasserstein}

% Source: nd_math_learning_project/probability/distribution/discrepency/kind/distance/kind/wasserstein/wasserstein.tex

The Wasserstein distance provides a metric between probability distributions
    \citep{vaserstein-1969-markov-processes-over-denumerable-products-of-spaces-describing-large-systems-of-automata}.
    
    
    \ProjectDeepHeading{5}{Gaussian}

\ProjectDeepHeading{3}{Gaussian}

% Source: nd_math_learning_project/probability/distribution/discrepency/kind/distance/kind/wasserstein/gaussian/gaussian.tex

For Gaussian distributions, the corresponding closed-form Fr{\'e}chet/Wasserstein-2
    distance can be computed from their means and covariance matrices
    \cite{dowson-1982-the-frechet-distance-between-multivariate-normal-distributions}.
    
    
    \ProjectDeepHeading{6}{Wasserstein Distance Between Two Gaussian Distributions}
        
        Suppose that we have two Gaussian distributions:
        
        \[
            P_1
            =
            \mathcal{N}
            \left(
                \ensuremath{\mu}_1,
                \ensuremath{\Sigma}_1
            \right)
        \]
        
        \[
            P_2
            =
            \mathcal{N}
            \left(
                \ensuremath{\mu}_2,
                \ensuremath{\Sigma}_2
            \right)
        \]
        
        where:
        
        \[
            \ensuremath{\mu}_1, \ensuremath{\mu}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{d}
        \]
        
        \[
            \ensuremath{\Sigma}_1, \ensuremath{\Sigma}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}
        \]
        
        The implemented distance is the second-order Wasserstein distance between two Gaussian distributions. Its squared form is:
        
        \[
            W_2^2
            \left(
                P_1,
                P_2
            \right)
            =
            \left\lVert
                \ensuremath{\mu}_1 - \ensuremath{\mu}_2
            \right\rVert_2^2
            +
            \operatorname{Tr}
            \left(
                \ensuremath{\Sigma}_1
            +
                \ensuremath{\Sigma}_2
            -
            2
                \left(
                    \ensuremath{\Sigma}_2^{1/2}
                    \ensuremath{\Sigma}_1
                    \ensuremath{\Sigma}_2^{1/2}
                \right)^{1/2}
            \right)
        \]
        
        Therefore, the actual Wasserstein distance is:
        
        \[
            W_2
            \left(
                P_1,
                P_2
            \right)
            =
            \sqrt{
                W_2^2
                \left(
                    P_1,
                    P_2
                \right)
            }
        \]
        
        Equivalently:
        
        \[
            W_2
            \left(
                P_1,
                P_2
            \right)
            =
            \sqrt{
                \left\lVert
                    \ensuremath{\mu}_1 - \ensuremath{\mu}_2
                \right\rVert_2^2
                +
                \operatorname{Tr}
                \left(
                    \ensuremath{\Sigma}_1
                +
                    \ensuremath{\Sigma}_2
                -
                2
                    \left(
                        \ensuremath{\Sigma}_2^{1/2}
                        \ensuremath{\Sigma}_1
                        \ensuremath{\Sigma}_2^{1/2}
                    \right)^{1/2}
                \right)
            }
        \]
    
    
    \ProjectDeepHeading{6}{Mean Distance Term}
        
        The first part of the distance measures how far the two Gaussian centers are from each other:
        
        \[
            d_{\ensuremath{\mu}}^2
            =
            \left\lVert
                \ensuremath{\mu}_1 - \ensuremath{\mu}_2
            \right\rVert_2^2
        \]
        
        If we define:
        
        \[
            \ensuremath{\Delta} \ensuremath{\mu}
            =
            \ensuremath{\mu}_1 - \ensuremath{\mu}_2
        \]
        
        then:
        
        \[
            d_{\ensuremath{\mu}}^2
            =
            \ensuremath{\Delta} \ensuremath{\mu}^T
            \ensuremath{\Delta} \ensuremath{\mu}
        \]
        
        This corresponds to the Euclidean squared distance between the two mean vectors.
    
    
    \ProjectDeepHeading{6}{Covariance Distance Term}
        
        The second part measures the difference between the covariance matrices:
        
        \[
            d_{\ensuremath{\Sigma}}^2
            =
            \operatorname{Tr}
            \left(
                \ensuremath{\Sigma}_1
            +
                \ensuremath{\Sigma}_2
            -
            2
                \left(
                    \ensuremath{\Sigma}_2^{1/2}
                    \ensuremath{\Sigma}_1
                    \ensuremath{\Sigma}_2^{1/2}
                \right)^{1/2}
            \right)
        \]
        
        This term compares the shape, spread, and orientation of the two Gaussian distributions.
        
        The code first computes:
        
        \[
            \ensuremath{\Sigma}_2^{1/2}
        \]
        
        Then it constructs the inner matrix:
        
        \[
            A
            =
            \ensuremath{\Sigma}_2^{1/2}
            \ensuremath{\Sigma}_1
            \ensuremath{\Sigma}_2^{1/2}
        \]
        
        Then it computes the symmetric matrix square root:
        
        \[
            A^{1/2}
            =
            \left(
                \ensuremath{\Sigma}_2^{1/2}
                \ensuremath{\Sigma}_1
                \ensuremath{\Sigma}_2^{1/2}
            \right)^{1/2}
        \]
        
        Finally, the covariance distance term becomes:
        
        \[
            d_{\ensuremath{\Sigma}}^2
            =
            \operatorname{Tr}
            \left(
                \ensuremath{\Sigma}_1
            +
                \ensuremath{\Sigma}_2
            -
            2A^{1/2}
            \right)
        \]
    
    
    \ProjectDeepHeading{6}{Final Distance}
        
        The final squared distance is the sum of the mean distance term and the covariance distance term:
        
        \[
            W_2^2
            \left(
                P_1,
                P_2
            \right)
            =
            d_{\ensuremath{\mu}}^2
            +
            d_{\ensuremath{\Sigma}}^2
        \]
        
        Therefore:
        
        \[
            W_2
            \left(
                P_1,
                P_2
            \right)
            =
            \sqrt{
                d_{\ensuremath{\mu}}^2
                +
                d_{\ensuremath{\Sigma}}^2
            }
        \]
    
    
    \ProjectDeepHeading{6}{Symmetric Matrix Square Root}
        
        For a symmetric positive semi-definite matrix \(\ensuremath{\Sigma}\), the eigendecomposition is:
        
        \[
            \ensuremath{\Sigma}
            =
            Q
            \ensuremath{\Lambda}
            Q^T
        \]
        
        where \(Q\) contains the eigenvectors and \(\ensuremath{\Lambda}\) is the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues:
        
        \[
            \ensuremath{\Lambda}
            =
            \operatorname{diag}
            \left(
                \ensuremath{\lambda}_1,
                \ensuremath{\lambda}_2,
                \ldots,
                \ensuremath{\lambda}_d
            \right)
        \]
        
        The square root of \(\ensuremath{\Sigma}\) is computed as:
        
        \[
            \ensuremath{\Sigma}^{1/2}
            =
            Q
            \ensuremath{\Lambda}^{1/2}
            Q^T
        \]
        
        with:
        
        \[
            \ensuremath{\Lambda}^{1/2}
            =
            \operatorname{diag}
            \left(
                \sqrt{\ensuremath{\lambda}_1},
                \sqrt{\ensuremath{\lambda}_2},
                \ldots,
                \sqrt{\ensuremath{\lambda}_d}
            \right)
        \]
        
        Because numerical errors may produce very small negative eigenvalues, the implementation clips them:
        
        \[
            \ensuremath{\lambda}_i^{+}
            =
            \max
            \left(
                \ensuremath{\lambda}_i,
            0
            \right)
        \]
        
        Thus, the implemented matrix square root is:
        
        \[
            \ensuremath{\Sigma}^{1/2}
            =
            Q
            \operatorname{diag}
            \left(
                \sqrt{\ensuremath{\lambda}_1^{+}},
                \sqrt{\ensuremath{\lambda}_2^{+}},
                \ldots,
                \sqrt{\ensuremath{\lambda}_d^{+}}
            \right)
            Q^T
        \]
    
    
    \ProjectDeepHeading{6}{Direction Between Two Gaussian Means}
        
        The method for direction does not use covariance matrices. It only computes the vector from the second mean to the first mean:
        
        \[
            v
            =
            \ensuremath{\mu}_1
            -
            \ensuremath{\mu}_2
        \]
        
        This vector gives the direction of displacement between the centers of the two Gaussian distributions.
    
    
    \ProjectDeepHeading{6}{One-Dimensional Case}
        
        For one-dimensional Gaussian distributions:
        
        \[
            P_1
            =
            \mathcal{N}
            \left(
                \ensuremath{\mu}_1,
                \ensuremath{\sigma}_1^2
            \right)
        \]
        
        \[
            P_2
            =
            \mathcal{N}
            \left(
                \ensuremath{\mu}_2,
                \ensuremath{\sigma}_2^2
            \right)
        \]
        
        the Wasserstein distance simplifies to:
        
        \[
            W_2^2
            \left(
                P_1,
                P_2
            \right)
            =
            \left(
                \ensuremath{\mu}_1
            -
                \ensuremath{\mu}_2
            \right)^2
            +
            \left(
                \ensuremath{\sigma}_1
            -
                \ensuremath{\sigma}_2
            \right)^2
        \]
        
        and:
        
        \[
            W_2
            \left(
                P_1,
                P_2
            \right)
            =
            \sqrt{
                \left(
                    \ensuremath{\mu}_1
                -
                    \ensuremath{\mu}_2
                \right)^2
                +
                \left(
                    \ensuremath{\sigma}_1
                -
                    \ensuremath{\sigma}_2
                \right)^2
            }
        \]
        
        This shows that, in one dimension, the distance has two components: the difference between means and the difference between standard deviations.

\subsubsection{Non parametric}

% Source: nd_math_learning_project/probability/distribution/non_parametric/empirical_probability_distribution.tex

An empirical probability distribution is a non-parametric probability distribution constructed directly from observed samples, without assuming
      a predefined parametric form for the underlying distribution \cite{wasserman-2006-all-of-nonparametric-statistics}.

      Given observations
      \[
      x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_N,
      \]
      the empirical probability measure is defined as

      \[
      \hat{\ensuremath{\mu}}_N
      =
      \frac{1}{N}
      \sum_{i=1}^{N}
      \ensuremath{\delta}_{x_i},
      \]

      where $\ensuremath{\delta}_{x_i}$ denotes the Dirac measure concentrated at observation
      $x_i$. Thus, each observed sample is assigned probability mass $1/N$.

\section{Statistics}

\subsection{Distance}

% Source: nd_math_learning_project/statistics/distance/distance.tex

\begin{minipage}{\textwidth}
        
        \begin{center}
            {\LARGE Taxonomy of Distance and Divergence Measures}
        \end{center}
        
        \vspace{1em}
        
        
        \subparagraph*{Overview}
            Distance and divergence measures quantify dissimilarity between mathematical objects (points, sets, functions, or probability distributions). These measures arise in different branches of mathematics. For example, \emph{Euclidean distance} comes from classical geometry, \emph{Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence} from information theory, and \emph{Hausdorff distance} from metric geometry/topology. A \emph{distance} in the strict sense usually means a metric satisfying symmetry and the triangle inequality, while a \emph{divergence} may lack those properties (e.g.\ KL divergence is not symmetric). Below is a structured categorization of common distance/divergence measures by their mathematical origin, with emphasis on comparing time series, spatial trajectories, or probability distributions.
        
        
        \subparagraph*{Branches of Mathematics vs.\ Example Distances}
            
            \begin{center}
                \begin{tabular}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{5cm} p{9cm}}
                    \toprule
                    \textbf{Mathematical Field} & \textbf{Distance / Divergence Measures} \\
                    \midrule
                    Metric Geometry (Normed Spaces) &
                    Euclidean ($L^2$), Manhattan ($L^1$), Minkowski ($L^p$), Chebyshev ($L^\infty$), Mahalanobis \\
                    
                    Discrete Mathematics (Coding Theory) &
                    Hamming distance, Levenshtein (edit) distance, Jaccard distance \\
                    
                    Topology / Geometry (Sets \& Curves) &
                    Hausdorff distance, Fr\'echet distance \\
                    
                    Time-Series Analysis (Alignment) &
                    Dynamic Time Warping (DTW), Longest Common Subsequence (LCSS) \\
                    
                    Probability \& Statistics &
                    Total variation distance, Hellinger distance, Mahalanobis distance \\
                    
                    Information Theory &
                    Kullback--Leibler divergence, Jensen--Shannon divergence, Bhattacharyya distance \\
                    
                    Optimal Transport (Measure Theory) &
                    Wasserstein distance (Earth Mover's Distance) \\
                    \bottomrule
                \end{tabular}
            \end{center}
        
        
        \subparagraph*{Metric Geometry: Norm-Based Distances}
            Metric geometry deals with distances in geometric spaces. These distances are induced by vector norms and satisfy the axioms of a metric.
            
            \ProjectDeepHeading{1}{Euclidean Distance ($L^2$)}
                The standard distance in Euclidean space, defined as
                \[
                    d(p,q) = \sqrt{\sum_i (p_i - q_i)^2}.
                \]
                It measures straight-line distance and is commonly used when time series are aligned.
            
            \ProjectDeepHeading{1}{Manhattan Distance ($L^1$)}
                Defined as
                \[
                    d(p,q) = \sum_i |p_i - q_i|.
                \]
                It is less sensitive to outliers than Euclidean distance.
            
            \ProjectDeepHeading{1}{Minkowski Distance}
                A general family of distances:
                \[
                    d_p(p,q) = \left( \sum_i |p_i - q_i|^p \right)^{1/p}.
                \]
            
            \ProjectDeepHeading{1}{Mahalanobis Distance}
                Accounts for feature covariance:
                \[
                    d_M(x,\ensuremath{\mu}) = \sqrt{(x-\ensuremath{\mu})^T \ensuremath{\Sigma}^{-1} (x-\ensuremath{\mu})}.
                \]
                It is widely used in statistics and anomaly detection.
            
            \ProjectDeepHeading{1}{Hamming and Jaccard Distances}
                Hamming distance counts mismatches in symbolic sequences, while Jaccard distance measures dissimilarity between sets:
                \[
                    d_J(A,B) = 1 - \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|}.
                \]
        
        
        \subparagraph*{Time-Series and Trajectory Distances}
            
            \ProjectDeepHeading{1}{Dynamic Time Warping (DTW)}
                DTW aligns sequences with different temporal speeds by minimizing a warping cost while preserving order.
            
            \ProjectDeepHeading{1}{Fr\'echet Distance}
                Measures similarity between curves while respecting ordering along the path.
            
            \ProjectDeepHeading{1}{Hausdorff Distance}
                A set-based metric measuring the maximum deviation between two point sets.
        
        
        \subparagraph*{Probability and Information-Theoretic Measures}
            
            \ProjectDeepHeading{1}{Total Variation and Hellinger Distance}
                Both are true metrics on probability distributions.
            
            \ProjectDeepHeading{1}{Kullback--Leibler Divergence}
                \[
                    D_{KL}(P\|Q) = \int p(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\,dx.
                \]
                It is asymmetric and not a metric.
            
            \ProjectDeepHeading{1}{Jensen--Shannon Divergence}
                A symmetric and bounded variant of KL divergence. Its square root is a metric.
            
            \ProjectDeepHeading{1}{Wasserstein Distance}
                An optimal transport metric measuring the minimal cost to transform one distribution into another.
        
        
        \subparagraph*{Conclusion}
            Different distance and divergence measures originate from different mathematical traditions. The appropriate choice depends on whether one compares aligned signals, trajectories, or probability distributions, and whether metric properties or information-theoretic interpretation is required.
    
    \end{minipage}

\subsubsection{Timeseries}

\paragraph{Motif discovery}

% Source: nd_math_learning_project/statistics/sequence/timeseries/motif_discovery/motif_discovery.tex

Motif discovery is the process of finding repeated or highly similar subsequences within time-series or sequential data. It is mainly used to identify recurring patterns without predefined labels. A motif describes what patterns frequently reappear in a sequence.

   \cite{guerrini-2025-time-series-motif-discovery-a-comprehensive-evaluation} present a comprehensive evaluation of time-series motif discovery, where the goal is to find recurring subsequences without prior knowledge of their shape or location. The paper reviews motif definitions, practical challenges, and 55 methods, then organizes them into frequency-based, similarity-based, and encoding-based families. Through experiments on real and synthetic datasets, the authors show that no single method is universally best; algorithm choice depends on motif length variation, noise, scalability, and the number of motifs.




   \ProjectDeepHeading{2}{Methods}
      \ProjectDeepHeading{3}{VALMOD}
         \cite{linardi-2018-matrix-profile-x-valmod-scalable-discovery-of-variable-length-motifs-in-data-series} introduces VALMOD, an exact and scalable method for discovering variable-length motifs in time/data series. It addresses the limitation of fixed-length motif discovery by searching over a length range and using lower bounds to avoid brute-force computation. The method is evaluated on diverse real datasets and is reported to be up to 20 times faster than previous state-of-the-art approaches.

\subparagraph{Matrix profile based}

% Source: nd_math_learning_project/statistics/sequence/timeseries/motif_discovery/matrix_profile_based/matrix_profiled_based.tex

\cite{vanonsem-2023-variable-length-motif-discovery-in-time-series-data} proposes a Matrix-Profile-based method for discovering variable-length motifs in noisy and periodic time series. Unlike VALMOD, it aims to return unique motifs together with all their occurrences, while also handling seasonal/repeating patterns. Its benchmarks on synthetic, Numenta taxi, and telecom KPI datasets show that it can detect both short and long motifs with one distance matrix calculation.

      \noindent
      \textbf{Input time series.}
      The method starts with a univariate time series.

      \begin{align}
         T &= (t_1,t_2,\dots,t_n)
      \end{align}

      \noindent
      Here, \(T\) is the input time series, \(t_i\) is the value at index \(i\), and \(n\) is the number of samples.

      \noindent
      \textbf{Initial subsequences.}
      A fixed initial window length \(w\) is used to extract short subsequences. This \(w\) is only the base comparison length, not necessarily the final motif length.

      \begin{align}
         S_i^{(w)} &= (t_i,t_{i+1},\dots,t_{i+w-1})
      \end{align}

      \noindent
      Here, \(S_i^{(w)}\) is the subsequence of length \(w\) starting at index \(i\).

      \noindent
      \textbf{Z-normalized Euclidean distance.}
      Two subsequences are first compared by their normalized shape.

      \begin{align}
         D_{\mathrm{z}}(S_i^{(w)},S_j^{(w)})
         &=
         \sqrt{
         \sum_{l=0}^{w-1}
         \left(
         \frac{t_{i+l}-\ensuremath{\mu}_i}{\ensuremath{\sigma}_i}
         -
         \frac{t_{j+l}-\ensuremath{\mu}_j}{\ensuremath{\sigma}_j}
         \right)^2
         }
      \end{align}

      \noindent
      Here, \(\ensuremath{\mu}_i\) and \(\ensuremath{\sigma}_i\) are the mean and standard deviation of \(S_i^{(w)}\), and \(\ensuremath{\mu}_j\) and \(\ensuremath{\sigma}_j\) are the mean and standard deviation of \(S_j^{(w)}\). A smaller \(D_{\mathrm{z}}\) means that the two subsequences have more similar shapes.

      \noindent
      \textbf{Scale difference.}
      The method also measures whether two subsequences have similar prominence or amplitude.

      \begin{align}
         D_{\mathrm{scale}}(S_i^{(w)},S_j^{(w)})
         &=
         \frac{
         \max\left(\operatorname{std}(S_i^{(w)}),\operatorname{std}(S_j^{(w)})\right)
         }{
         \min\left(\operatorname{std}(S_i^{(w)}),\operatorname{std}(S_j^{(w)})\right)
         }
         -1
      \end{align}

      \noindent
      Here, \(D_{\mathrm{scale}}\) is close to zero when the two subsequences have similar standard deviations. It becomes larger when one subsequence is much more prominent than the other.

      \noindent
      \textbf{Capped scale difference.}
      The scale distance is capped to avoid an unlimited effect of amplitude difference.

      \begin{align}
         D_{\mathrm{scale,capped}}(S_i^{(w)},S_j^{(w)})
         &=
         \frac{
         \min\left(D_{\mathrm{scale}}(S_i^{(w)},S_j^{(w)}),c\right)
         }{c}
      \end{align}

      \noindent
      Here, \(c\) is the cap parameter. This produces a bounded scale term.

      \noindent
      \textbf{Scale-aware distance.}
      The final distance combines normalized shape distance and capped scale distance.

      \begin{align}
         D_{\mathrm{aware}}(S_i^{(w)},S_j^{(w)})
         &=
         \frac{
         \sqrt{
         \left(
         \frac{D_{\mathrm{z}}(S_i^{(w)},S_j^{(w)})}{2\sqrt{w}}
         \right)^2
         +
         D_{\mathrm{scale,capped}}(S_i^{(w)},S_j^{(w)})^2
         }
         }{\sqrt{2}}
      \end{align}

      \noindent
      Here, \(D_{\mathrm{aware}}\) is small only when two subsequences are similar in both shape and scale.

      \noindent
      \textbf{Pairwise distance matrix.}
      The distance between every pair of initial subsequences is stored in a matrix.

      \begin{align}
         M_{ij}
         &=
         D_{\mathrm{aware}}(S_i^{(w)},S_j^{(w)})
      \end{align}

      \noindent
      Here, \(M_{ij}\) is the distance between the subsequence starting at \(i\) and the subsequence starting at \(j\).

      \noindent
      \textbf{Binary event matrix.}
      A threshold \(\ensuremath{\tau}\) is applied to the distance matrix. A match below the threshold is called an event.

      \begin{align}
         B_{ij}
         &=
         \begin{cases}
            1, & M_{ij}\leq \ensuremath{\tau},\\
            0, & M_{ij}>\ensuremath{\tau}.
         \end{cases}
      \end{align}

      \noindent
      Here, \(B_{ij}=1\) means that \(S_i^{(w)}\) and \(S_j^{(w)}\) are similar enough to be treated as a local match.

      \noindent
      \textbf{Diagonal ranking.}
      Each diagonal corresponds to a fixed temporal shift \(k\). The method counts the number of events on each diagonal.

      \begin{align}
         R(k)
         &=
         \sum_i B_{i,i+k}
      \end{align}

      \noindent
      Here, \(R(k)\) is the number of matching events on diagonal \(k\). A larger \(R(k)\) means that more repeated local matches exist with the same temporal shift.

      \noindent
      \textbf{Best diagonal.}
      The diagonal with the largest number of events is processed first.

      \begin{align}
         k^\star
         &=
         \arg\max_k R(k)
      \end{align}

      \noindent
      Here, \(k^\star\) is the highest-ranked diagonal.

      \noindent
      \textbf{Candidate events.}
      The matching positions on a selected diagonal form the initial motif-candidate evidence.

      \begin{align}
         C_{k^\star}
         &=
         \left\{
         (i,i+k^\star)
         \mid
         B_{i,i+k^\star}=1
         \right\}
      \end{align}

      \noindent
      Here, \(C_{k^\star}\) is the set of event positions on the selected diagonal. Consecutive or near-consecutive events suggest a longer repeated segment.

      \noindent
      \textbf{Variable-length motif candidate.}
      The candidate is enlarged along the diagonal, but its length cannot exceed the diagonal shift, because otherwise the two occurrences would overlap.

      \begin{align}
         L_{\mathrm{candidate}}
         &\leq
         k^\star
      \end{align}

      \noindent
      Here, \(L_{\mathrm{candidate}}\) is the length of the enlarged motif candidate.

      \noindent
      \textbf{Candidate validation.}
      The enlarged candidate is accepted only if the two enlarged subsequences still satisfy the distance threshold.

      \begin{align}
         D_{\mathrm{aware}}(S_a^{(L)},S_b^{(L)})
         &\leq
         \ensuremath{\tau}
      \end{align}

      \noindent
      Here, \(S_a^{(L)}\) and \(S_b^{(L)}\) are the two enlarged subsequences of length \(L\). If this condition holds, the candidate is accepted as a motif.

      \noindent
      \textbf{Occurrence grouping.}
      After a motif is accepted, all similar occurrences are collected under the same motif label.

      \begin{align}
         \mathcal{O}_m
         &=
         \left\{
         a_r
         \mid
         D_{\mathrm{aware}}(S_{a_r}^{(L_m)},S_m^{(L_m)})\leq \ensuremath{\tau}
         \right\}
      \end{align}

      \noindent
      Here, \(\mathcal{O}_m\) is the set of start indices of all occurrences of motif \(m\), \(L_m\) is the length of motif \(m\), and \(S_m^{(L_m)}\) is a representative occurrence.

      \noindent
      \textbf{Compact pipeline.}

      \begin{align}
         T
         \rightarrow
         \{S_i^{(w)}\}
         \rightarrow
         M
         \rightarrow
         B
         \rightarrow
         \text{diagonal events}
         \rightarrow
         \text{variable-length candidates}
         \rightarrow
         \text{grouped motif occurrences}
      \end{align}

      \noindent
      The central idea is that the fixed window \(w\) is only used to detect local matching events. Longer motifs are recovered by connecting events along diagonals of the pairwise distance matrix.

\subparagraph{Gru autoencoder based}

% Source: nd_math_learning_project/statistics/sequence/timeseries/motif_discovery/gru_autoencoder_based/gru_autoencoder_based.tex

\cite{bascol-2016-unsupervised-interpretable-pattern-discovery-in-time-series-using-autoencoders} propose an unsupervised method for discovering recurrent temporal patterns in multivariate time series using convolutional autoencoders .
   The convolutional filters learn temporal patterns directly from the input sequences without requiring labeled motif examples. The architecture introduces an adaptive rectified linear activation to improve the interpretability of the discovered patterns. A group-lasso regularization term is used to suppress redundant filters and automatically retain a relevant set of recurrent patterns. The method is evaluated on synthetic and real activity data and demonstrates that autoencoders can be used for unsupervised temporal pattern discovery.

\paragraph{Similarity measure}

\subparagraph{Kind}

\ProjectDeepHeading{1}{Dynamic time warping}

% Source: nd_math_learning_project/statistics/sequence/timeseries/similarity_measure/kind/dynamic_time_warping/dynamic_time_warping.tex

\seeherefooter{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_time_warping} for soem implementations
   Dynamic Time Warping is a time-series similarity method used to compare two sequences that may have similar shapes but different local speeds.

   Let

   \[
   X
   =
   (
   x_1,
   x_2,
   \ldots,
   x_n
   )
   \]

   and

   \[
   Y
   =
   (
   y_1,
   y_2,
   \ldots,
   y_m
   )
   \]

   be two time series. DTW finds an alignment path between \(X\) and \(Y\) by minimizing the cumulative matching cost.

   \[
   D(i,j)
   =
   d(x_i,y_j)
   +
   \min
   \left\{
   D(i-1,j),
   D(i,j-1),
   D(i-1,j-1)
   \right\}
   \]

   where \(d(x_i,y_j)\) is the local distance between two samples.

   The final DTW distance is

   \[
   \mathrm{DTW}(X,Y)
   =
   D(n,m)
   \]

   Unlike Euclidean distance, DTW does not compare only points with the same index. It allows one point in a sequence to be matched with one or more nearby points in the other sequence.

   Therefore, DTW is useful when two time series represent the same pattern but are shifted, stretched, or compressed in time.
